To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the spin structure of the proton has been measured at Q^2 = 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.5, 8.5, and 10.0 GeV^2.

the proton structure functions F 2 and F 3 have been measured with high precision over a wide range in x and Q 2, and that the asymmetries A 1 and A 3 are positive, large, and in agreement with the predictions of quark parton models.
the asymmetries in deep inelastic electron-proton scattering are large and positive and that there is no significant asymmetry in the scattering of polarized photons from unpolarized nucleon targets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the structure of the proton and neutron, and the study of the weak interactions of leptons.
a study of the spin-dependent structure of the proton.
the measurement of the spin asymmetry in the scattering of polarized 3.5-GeV electrons by polarized 50-GeV protons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are consistent with the quark-parton model and with the hypothesis that the weak interaction is parity-conserving.
the data are consistent with the quark model, but are not inconsistent with the possibility of a small parity nonconservation effect.
the data are consistent with a simple quark model of the proton.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proton is made of quarks and that the quarks carry a significant fraction of the proton momentum.
we have measured a new fundamental property of the proton and that we have established the validity of the quark-parton model of the proton in the deep inelastic regime.
we have measured the parity-violating asymmetry of deep inelastic scattering, A_{PV} = 0.0019 +/- 0.0020 (statistical) +/- 0.0010 (systematic).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quarks inside the proton are polarized, and that this polarization is in agreement with the predictions of the Standard Model.
it is possible to use the polarization asymmetry in deep-inelastic scattering to measure the parity-violating weak force.
we are able to measure the proton spin structure function, g1, with unprecedented precision.
